sentences.text: Kayrasaurus was a medium-sized therizinosaur, reaching at least 3.6 meters in length and weighing between 117 and 274 kilograms.
Its furcula formed a broad V shape with an angle of about 140 degrees, a typical feature of therizinosaurs.
The humerus was notably stout and straight, unlike the curved version seen in Falcarius, and resembled that of Erliansaurus and Nothronychus graffami.
The radius was slender and straight, matching the condition in basal therizinosaurs.
The iliac blade displayed a sub-parallelogram outline in side view, a shape shared with basal therizinosaurs, early birds, and dromaeosaurids.
Its ischiadic peduncle was peg-like, differing from the more derived square or circular forms.
CT scans show the skull was extremely flattened, measuring only 3 to 5 millimeters in thickness.
Ten neck vertebrae are preserved in their original order, providing a rare glimpse of the cervical series.
The neck bones were pneumatized, indicated by air-filled openings on their sides.
Fossils were recovered from outcrops near Dabangou village, close to Beipiao in Liaoning Province, China, within the Yixian Formation.
The type locality for the species is the Yixian Formation, and the genus was formally named by Liao and colleagues in 2026.
Only a single species, Kayrasaurus changliensis, is known, based on a nearly complete skeleton that includes the skull.
The specimen lacks most of the leg bones and much of the pelvis, leaving those parts unknown.
The Paleobiology Database records just one fossil occurrence of this taxon.
Most teeth were uniform in size, although the anterior teeth were probably larger, suggesting a gradation in feeding function.
The front of the jaws lacked teeth, a condition shared with other therizinosaurs.
Its close relatives include the contemporaneous Beipiaosaurus and Jianchangosaurus, indicating a diverse therizinosaur community in the Jehol Biota.
Kayrasaurus occupies an early-branching position within Therizinosauria, the broader therizinosaur group.
It belongs to the class Reptilia.
The animal lived during the Early Cretaceous Barremian to Aptian ages, roughly 125.77 to 119.57 million years ago, in what is now the Yixian Formation of China.
Scientists are uncertain whether the known specimen represents a fully grown adult, as it may have been a subadult individual.
